title: AI Detectors Are Out, New Approaches Are In rs-are-out-new-approaches-are
author: Kathryn Palmer
summary: Kathryn Palmer reports for Inside Higher Ed on why a growing number of universities are abandoning AI detectors and pushing faculty to redesign assessments instead. She cites studies showing detectors are inconsistent, produce false positives and are biased against non-native English writers, with some accused students suing. Institutions including Yale, Vanderbilt, Johns Hopkins and Indiana discourage relying on detectors, and at least a dozen have disabled Turnitin's AI detection. Yale's teaching center adds that humanizing tools defeat detection, turning enforcement into a cat and mouse game. Experts such as Kevin Yee, Marc Watkins and Tricia Bertram Gallant argue that faculty must move toward AI-resilient assignments, oral exams and supervised assessment, although the labor cost is large. The piece frames the shift as an acknowledgment that unsupervised written work no longer reliably shows learning.
points: Detector unreliability, false positives and lawsuits are pushing institutions to ban or discourage detector-only cheating cases.
Humanizing tools make detection an arms race, which Yale says turns academic integrity into a technical exercise rather than a learning event.
Small in-person classes can rely on relationships, while larger classes need AI-resilient redesigns such as blue book or oral exams.
Faculty can use an LLM to help rework assignments, which lowers the burden of redesign.
Bertram Gallant argues that unsupervised written work no longer validly measures learning, so assessment should move to temptation-free settings.
quotes: Numerous studies have shown that AI detectors—such as those developed by OpenAI, Writer, Copyleaks, GPTZero and CrossPlag—exhibit inconsistencies, produce false positives when evaluating human-generated writing and are biased against non-native English writers. In some cases, those false positives have resulted in accused students filing lawsuits against their universities.
Instead of trying to ‘catch’ AI use, focus on designing assignments that encourage process, reasoning, and authentic engagement.

We want to avoid the inevitable cat and mouse game created by AI detection tools: As the tools get better at ‘catching’ AI generated text, so do methods to evade detection. This becomes a technical exercise rather than a learning event.
If faculty had an AI detector that was reliable, that’s what they would use. But many are reluctantly moving in the direction of assignment redesign because they are at wit’s end

In larger classes, there’s less of a personal connection between students and faculty, so faculty need to redesign their assessments to be more AI-resilient or a completely kind of deliverable that AI can’t do, such as a blue book exam or an in-person oral exam.
We’re still relying on the unsupervised written word as evidence of learning. The real trick is acknowledging that that doesn’t work anymore.

We cannot be giving unsupervised assessments to students expecting them to resist AI. They’re not going to be learning, we’re going to be spending our time trying to catch them cheating and they’re going to graduate and realize they just wasted four years,
